analysis.one_liner: Gives college athletes federal collective bargaining rights as employees.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in December 2023, referred to the Senate health and labor committee, and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change the National Labor Relations Act so that college athletes who receive scholarships or other pay tied to playing a sport count as employees with the right to unionize. Athletes could form bargaining units across all the schools in an athletic conference, negotiate over pay, health and safety, and working conditions, and no school could require them to sign away those rights. The bill also spells out that none of this changes athletes' tax treatment or their eligibility for federal financial aid.
analysis.who_benefits: College athletes, especially those in the revenue sports (football and basketball) that generate billions for their schools. The bill's findings note intercollegiate sports generate more than $15 billion a year while athletes themselves are capped in what they can earn, cannot negotiate collectively, and can lose their eligibility for breaking NCAA terms [S2]. Unionizing would let them bargain over compensation, health and safety protections, and rules set conference-wide, and would bar schools from making athletes waive these rights in scholarship agreements [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Classifies college athletes who receive any direct compensation, including scholarships, as employees under the National Labor Relations Act, giving them the right to organize and bargain collectively [S2].

Extends the law to public universities as well as private ones, and allows bargaining units that span all the schools in an athletic conference, since rules like compensation caps and transfer limits are typically set conference-wide [S2].
Prohibits any agreement, including a scholarship agreement or legal settlement, that waives the rights this bill creates [S2].
Leaves athletes' tax treatment and federal financial aid eligibility unchanged, so a scholarship would not become taxable income or reduce aid because of this bill [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The NCAA, athletic conferences, and university athletic departments, which currently set compensation and playing terms without negotiating with athletes. If athletes unionized, schools in revenue sports would face collective bargaining over a share of sports revenue, health and safety standards, and limits on the rules they can impose unilaterally. Some of those costs could flow to athletic budgets that are partly subsidized by student fees and university funds.
analysis.who_pays_short: The NCAA, conferences, and university athletic departments

drawbacks.text: Critics argue college athletes are students, not employees, and that treating them as unionized workers could blur or end the amateur model that distinguishes college sports from professional leagues [S2].

Collective bargaining over pay could pressure athletic department budgets, some of which run deficits and rely on student fees, university subsidies, or donor money, potentially squeezing non-revenue sports [S2].

The bill excludes the NCAA from the definition of an athletic conference, leaving questions about how conference-level bargaining would interact with NCAA-wide rules, and extending federal labor law to public universities is a significant shift that courts could have tested [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change is real and plainly favors athletes: it would convert a one-sided relationship, where schools and the NCAA set the terms and athletes accept or lose eligibility, into a negotiated one. The main costs fall on institutions that currently keep the revenue, not on students or taxpayers generally, though athletic subsidies drawn from student fees are a fair worry. The design addresses the biggest practical objections up front (tax treatment, financial aid, waiver bans), but the multi-school conference bargaining structure was untested and would likely have drawn legal challenges.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Christopher Murphy introduced the bill on December 6, 2023, joined by Sen. Bernard Sanders and Sen. Elizabeth Warren [S1].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S4].
No further action appears in the record: no committee hearing, markup, floor vote, or House companion action, and the Congress ended January 3, 2025 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The NCAA, athletic conferences, and university athletic departments kept the status quo: college athletes remain outside federal labor law, so schools and conferences continue to set compensation and playing terms without collective bargaining. Athletes gained nothing from the bill's death.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The NCAA and university athletic departments

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.role: U.S. Senator from Massachusetts; original cosponsor

against.what_they_did: Received the bill on December 6, 2023 and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled.

against.name: Senate Republican conference
against.role: Senate majority (41+ members needed to advance most legislation)
against.what_they_did: No Republican cosponsored the bill, and the Senate majority took no action to bring it to the floor during the 118th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held, so no party breakdown exists; all three sponsors were Democrats or an Independent who caucuses with Democrats, and no Republican cosponsor joined [S3].

industries.industry: The NCAA and intercollegiate athletic conferences
industries.note: The bill would strip the NCAA and conferences of their power to cap athlete compensation and set playing terms without negotiation, and its findings describe their current practices as exploitative collusion on pay. Their interest in keeping that power runs directly against athletes' [S2].

Schools would have to bargain collectively over pay, health and safety, and rules, and could no longer require athletes to waive rights in scholarship agreements. Revenue-sport departments would share more of the money their sports generate [S2].

industries.industry: Labor unions and existing professional sports player associations
industries.note: The bill opens a large new group of potential union members and bargaining units, a role likely filled with help from established player associations. Their interest in organizing athletes runs alongside athletes' interest in representation [S2].
